title: What Photo 51 Could Say
topic: x-ray evidence and the structure of dna
paragraphs: The most famous image in the history of molecular biology is not a picture of anything a person would recognize.
Photo 51 is a dark field crossed by a blurred X of short dashes, with a heavy smudge at the top and another at the bottom, and to an untrained eye it could pass for a flaw in the film.
It was recorded at King's College London in May 1952, and within a year it had helped to settle one of the central questions of twentieth-century science: the shape of deoxyribonucleic acid, or DNA.
The story of that year is usually told as the triumph of two men in Cambridge, James Watson and Francis Crick, and their model deserves the admiration it has received.
But the model rested on measurements made by other people, and the question of how those measurements traveled from one laboratory to another has been argued over for seventy years.
DNA had been known for a long time without being taken seriously.
The Swiss chemist Friedrich Miescher isolated it from the nuclei of white blood cells in 1869 and named it nuclein.
In the early twentieth century the biochemist Phoebus Levene identified its parts: a sugar, a phosphate group, and four nitrogen-containing bases called adenine, guanine, cytosine, and thymine.

Levene proposed that the four bases simply repeated in a fixed order along the chain, a view known as the tetranucleotide hypothesis, and a molecule that monotonous seemed too dull to carry hereditary instructions.
Proteins, built from some twenty different amino acids, looked a far better candidate.
Two experiments changed the mood.

In 1944 Oswald Avery and his colleagues at the Rockefeller Institute showed that purified DNA could transfer a heritable trait from one strain of pneumonia bacteria to another, and in 1952 Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase showed that when a virus infects a bacterium, it is mainly the viral DNA, not the protein coat, that enters the cell.
The tetranucleotide hypothesis fell to careful chemistry.

Working at Columbia University in the late 1940s, Erwin Chargaff used the new technique of paper chromatography to separate the four bases from the DNA of many species and to measure how much of each was present.
He found two things.
First, the proportions of the bases differed from one species to another, which a fixed repeating unit could not allow.
Second, in every sample the amount of adenine closely matched the amount of thymine, and the amount of guanine closely matched the amount of cytosine.
These regularities became known as Chargaff's ratios.
Chargaff reported them without explaining them, and when he met Watson and Crick in Cambridge in 1952 he came away, by his own later account, unimpressed by their command of the chemistry.
The shape of the molecule was a question for a different technique.

When a beam of X-rays passes through a crystal, or through a fiber in which long molecules lie roughly parallel, the regularly spaced atoms scatter the beam into a pattern of spots and arcs that can be recorded on film.
The pattern is not an image of the molecule; it is a map of the distances that repeat inside it, and turning the map back into a structure takes mathematics and judgment.

In 1938 William Astbury and Florence Bell at the University of Leeds recorded the first X-ray patterns from DNA fibers and found a strong repeat of 3.4 angstroms along the fiber axis, an angstrom being one ten-billionth of a meter.
Astbury pictured the bases stacked flat like a pile of coins, but his fibers were too poorly ordered to tell him more.
The problem passed to King's College London, where the physicist John Randall had assembled a biophysics unit after the war.
Maurice Wilkins, Randall's deputy, had begun taking diffraction photographs of DNA fibers with a graduate student, Raymond Gosling, and had obtained sharper patterns than Astbury's.
In January 1951 Rosalind Franklin joined the unit.

Trained as a physical chemist at Cambridge, she had spent three years in Paris learning to apply X-ray methods to poorly crystalline materials, and Randall assigned her the DNA problem, with Gosling as her student.
Wilkins seems to have expected her to work as his assistant; she understood from Randall's letter that the problem was now hers.
The misunderstanding was never repaired, and the two worked in the same building with as little contact as they could manage.
Franklin's first discovery was that DNA fibers exist in two forms.

At lower humidity the molecule packs into an ordered, crystalline arrangement she called the A form; when the fibers take up water they loosen into a less ordered arrangement she called the B form, which is the state of DNA in a living cell.
Earlier photographs had been muddled because they caught both forms at once.

By controlling the moisture around the fiber, Franklin and Gosling could photograph each form on its own, and in May 1952 Gosling, working under her direction, recorded the image of the B form that became Photo 51.
To anyone trained in the diffraction theory of helices, which Crick and two colleagues had published that same year, the picture was eloquent.

The X of dashes meant a helix; the spacing between the dashes gave the distance the helix climbs in one full turn, 34 angstroms; the smudges at the top and bottom gave the 3.4 angstrom spacing between stacked bases; and the width of the pattern gave the molecule's diameter, about 20 angstroms.
The bases, it followed, were stacked ten to a turn.
Franklin did not rush to build a model.

The B form was plainly helical, but the A form, with its richer pattern, promised more exact information, and she set out to extract it by a slow method called Patterson analysis, which assumes nothing about the structure in advance.

She was skeptical of guesswork, and in July 1952 she and Gosling circulated a mock death notice for the crystalline DNA helix, a joke that has often been read, unfairly, as a denial that DNA was helical at all.
A draft she wrote in March 1953, before she had seen the Cambridge model, describes the B form as a helix of two chains with the phosphate groups on the outside.
What she lacked was not insight but a reason to hurry.
Watson and Crick, at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, worked in the opposite spirit.

Following the example of Linus Pauling, who had found the alpha helix of proteins in 1951 by building models that obeyed the known geometry of chemical bonds, they tried to guess the structure first and test it against the X-ray data afterward.
Their first attempt, in November 1951, was a three-chain helix with the phosphates on the inside.
Franklin, who came up from London to see it, pointed out that it allowed for only a fraction of the water her measurements showed the fibers to contain, and the model did not survive the visit.
Lawrence Bragg, who directed the laboratory, ordered the pair to leave DNA to King's.
They were let back in only in early 1953, after Pauling himself produced a three-chain model with the same flaw, and the thought that he would soon correct it made the race seem urgent.
Three pieces of evidence then crossed from London to Cambridge.
In January 1953 Wilkins showed Watson Photo 51 without telling Franklin, and Watson, who knew the helical theory, read the X at a glance.

In February Max Perutz, a senior Cavendish scientist who sat on a committee that reviewed the King's unit, gave Crick a report containing Franklin's measurements, among them the symmetry of the A form crystals, from which Crick deduced that the two chains ran in opposite directions.
Finally Jerry Donohue, an American chemist who shared their office, corrected the textbook forms of the bases that Watson had been using.

With the right forms, Watson found at the end of February that a pair made of adenine and thymine had the same width as a pair made of guanine and cytosine, so that any sequence of pairs could fit between two evenly spaced backbones.
Chargaff's ratios, unexplained for several years, fell out of the geometry at once: if adenine always faces thymine, the two must be equally abundant.
The result appeared in Nature on April 25, 1953, in a paper of about nine hundred words, alongside separate papers from Wilkins's group and from Franklin and Gosling.

Watson and Crick described two chains wound around a common axis, with the sugar and phosphate backbones outside and the paired bases inside, held together by hydrogen bonds, and they added one sentence that has been quoted ever since: that the specific pairing immediately suggested a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material.
They acknowledged being stimulated by a general knowledge of unpublished results from King's; they did not say how much they had seen.
Franklin had already left for Birkbeck College in London, where she turned to the structure of viruses and did some of her finest work.
She died of ovarian cancer in April 1958, at the age of thirty-seven.

In 1962 the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to Watson, Crick, and Wilkins; a prize is shared by at most three people and is not awarded to the dead, so the question of whether she would have been included was never put.
The argument over credit began in earnest in 1968, when Watson published The Double Helix, a memoir that treated Franklin as an obstacle and was condescending about her appearance and her temper.
Anne Sayre's biography of 1975 answered it, and a story took shape in which Franklin's photograph was stolen and her discovery taken from her.
That story is too simple, and I think it does her a disservice.

Her Birkbeck colleague Aaron Klug, reading her notebooks after her death, showed that she had worked out several main features of the double helix on her own and was, in his judgment, close to the full structure.

In 2023 the historians Matthew Cobb and Nathaniel Comfort argued, from a draft magazine article written in 1953 after interviews with Franklin, that she was better informed about the Cambridge work than the familiar story allows and should be seen as an equal member of a four-person team.
On that reading she was not a victim who never learned what had happened but a contributor whose share was quietly forgotten, which is a different wrong and in some ways a harder one to put right.
What strikes me most, reading the record, is how little a single image could settle.
Photo 51 said helix and gave three numbers; it did not say how many chains there were, which way they ran, or how the bases fit together.

Those answers came from the symmetry in Franklin's crystallographic report, from Chargaff's ratios, from Donohue's chemistry, and from the willingness of two impatient men to keep building models that were wrong until one was right.
The double helix was the meeting point of two methods, the patient measurement that Franklin practiced and the bold guessing that she distrusted, and neither would have finished the job alone.
That is a less satisfying story than a theft or a triumph, but I suspect it is the true one.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the tetranucleotide hypothesis made DNA seem an unlikely carrier of hereditary instructions because
choices: it suggested that DNA occurred only in the nuclei of blood cells
it held that DNA contained far fewer parts than the proteins it was compared with
it pictured the four bases repeating in a fixed order along the chain
it showed that the proportions of the bases differed from species to species
it proposed that the molecule was a single short chain rather than a long one

proof.quote: Levene proposed that the four bases simply repeated in a fixed order along the chain

questions.why: Paragraph 2 says Levene proposed that the four bases simply repeated in a fixed order along the chain, and that a molecule that monotonous seemed too dull to carry hereditary instructions.
distractorNotes: Wrong detail: white blood cells are where Miescher isolated DNA in paragraph 2, not part of Levene's hypothesis.
Half right: proteins had more building blocks, but the hypothesis was about the order of the bases, not a count of parts.
Reversed: paragraph 3 says Chargaff's finding that the proportions differ is exactly what the hypothesis could not allow.
Outside the passage: nothing is said about the length of the chain.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Chargaff's measurements showed that
choices: the amount of adenine in a sample closely matched the amount of thymine
the four bases were present in equal amounts in the DNA of every species
the DNA of all species contained the same proportions of the four bases
adenine and thymine together made up a fixed fraction of every sample
the bases could be separated only after the sugar had been removed

proof.quote: the amount of adenine closely matched the amount of thymine

questions.why: Paragraph 3 lists his two findings, and the second is that in every sample the amount of adenine closely matched the amount of thymine, and the amount of guanine closely matched the amount of cytosine.
distractorNotes: Too strong: only the paired bases matched each other; nothing says all four were present in equal amounts.
Reversed: paragraph 3 says the proportions differed from one species to another.
Outside the passage: no fixed fraction for adenine plus thymine is mentioned.
Outside the passage: paper chromatography separated the bases, and nothing is said about removing the sugar first.

questions.stem: The author describes how X-ray diffraction works in paragraph 4 primarily to
choices: argue that Astbury's photographs were more accurate than those taken later at King's
show that the technique was invented specifically to study the shape of DNA
explain why Franklin preferred to study the A form rather than the B form
establish that a diffraction pattern must be interpreted rather than simply viewed
demonstrate that the bases in DNA are stacked flat like a pile of coins

proof.quote: The pattern is not an image of the molecule; it is a map of the distances that repeat inside it

questions.why: Paragraph 4 says the pattern is not an image of the molecule but a map of repeating distances, and that turning it back into a structure takes mathematics and judgment. The description is there so the reader understands why reading Photo 51 took training.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 5 says Wilkins and Gosling obtained sharper patterns than Astbury's.
Outside the passage: the technique is described in general terms, and nothing says it was invented for DNA.
Wrong paragraph: Franklin's choice of the A form is explained in paragraph 7, and for a different reason.
Wrong purpose: the pile of coins is Astbury's guess about the bases, mentioned after the technique is explained, not the reason for explaining it.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the friction between Franklin and Wilkins arose because
choices: Randall had removed Wilkins from the biophysics unit before Franklin arrived
each of them understood a different person to be in charge of the DNA work
Franklin refused to share Gosling's earlier photographs with Wilkins
Wilkins had been trained in Paris and distrusted her Cambridge methods
Franklin had publicly criticized the quality of Wilkins's diffraction patterns

proof.quote: Wilkins seems to have expected her to work as his assistant; she understood from Randall's letter that the problem was now hers.

questions.why: Paragraph 5 says Wilkins expected her to work as his assistant while she understood from Randall's letter that the problem was hers, and that this misunderstanding was never repaired.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: Wilkins is described as Randall's deputy and stayed in the unit.
Outside the passage: nothing is said about Franklin withholding photographs.
Reversed: it was Franklin, not Wilkins, who had trained in Paris.
Outside the passage: no public criticism is mentioned; the two simply avoided each other.

questions.stem: According to the passage, all of the following could be read from Photo 51 EXCEPT:
choices: the distance the helix climbs in one full turn
the spacing between stacked bases
the diameter of the molecule
the fact that the molecule is a helix
the number of chains in the molecule

proof.quote: the spacing between the dashes gave the distance the helix climbs in one full turn
the 3.4 angstrom spacing between stacked bases
the width of the pattern gave the molecule's diameter
The X of dashes meant a helix
it did not say how many chains there were

questions.why: Paragraph 6 lists what the picture gave: a helix, the 34 angstrom rise per turn, the 3.4 angstrom spacing between bases, and the 20 angstrom diameter. Paragraph 12 says outright that it did not say how many chains there were.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 6 says the spacing between the dashes gave the distance the helix climbs in one full turn.
Paragraph 6 says the smudges at the top and bottom gave the spacing between stacked bases.
Paragraph 6 says the width of the pattern gave the molecule's diameter.
Paragraph 6 says the X of dashes meant a helix.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 6, the word 'eloquent' most nearly means
choices: fluently spoken
full of meaning
forcefully argued
pleasing to look at
hard to interpret

proof.quote: the picture was eloquent

questions.why: Paragraph 6 says the picture was eloquent to anyone trained in the diffraction theory of helices, and the next sentence lists everything it told such a reader. The image spoke volumes in the sense of carrying meaning, not in the sense of speech.
distractorNotes: This is the everyday sense of the word, but a photograph does not speak.
The picture is not making an argument; it is yielding information to a trained reader.
Paragraph 1 says the image could pass for a flaw in the film, so beauty is not the point.
Reversed: the sentence says the picture was clear to a trained reader, not hard to read.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the mock death notice circulated in July 1952 referred to
choices: the A form of the molecule rather than DNA in general
the three-chain model built in Cambridge the previous year
the B form, which Franklin had not yet photographed
Astbury's picture of the bases stacked like coins
the end of Franklin's collaboration with Gosling

proof.quote: a mock death notice for the crystalline DNA helix
ordered, crystalline arrangement she called the A form

questions.why: Paragraph 7 says the notice was for the crystalline DNA helix, and paragraph 6 identifies the crystalline arrangement as the A form. Put the two together and the joke was about the A form, which is why the author calls the broader reading unfair.
distractorNotes: Wrong target: the Cambridge model is in paragraph 8, and the notice concerns a form of DNA, not a model.
Contradicted: Photo 51, the image of the B form, was taken in May 1952, two months earlier.
Wrong paragraph: Astbury's picture is in paragraph 4 and has nothing to do with the notice.
Contradicted: Gosling circulated the notice with her, so the collaboration continued.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Franklin objected to the first Cambridge model because it
choices: put the phosphate groups on the outside of the helix
contained two chains when her data pointed to three
copied the three-chain structure that Pauling had already published
allowed for far less water than her measurements showed
placed the bases ten to a turn instead of eleven

proof.quote: it allowed for only a fraction of the water her measurements showed the fibers to contain

questions.why: Paragraph 8 says Franklin pointed out that the model allowed for only a fraction of the water her measurements showed the fibers to contain, and that the model did not survive the visit.
distractorNotes: Reversed: the first model had the phosphates on the inside.
Reversed: the model had three chains, and the passage never says her data pointed to three.
Wrong timing: Pauling's model came in early 1953, after the Cambridge attempt of November 1951.
Outside the passage: no count of bases per turn figures in her objection.

questions.stem: The author mentions Linus Pauling's alpha helix in paragraph 8 primarily to
choices: show that proteins had already been proven to be the true carriers of heredity
explain why Bragg ordered Watson and Crick to stop working on DNA
identify the method of model building that Watson and Crick were imitating
suggest that Pauling had already solved the structure of DNA by 1951
contrast the alpha helix of proteins with the double helix of DNA

proof.quote: Following the example of Linus Pauling, who had found the alpha helix of proteins in 1951 by building models

questions.why: Paragraph 8 introduces Pauling as the example Watson and Crick were following: build a model that obeys the known chemistry, then test it against the data. The alpha helix is there as proof that the method could work.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 2 says the experiments of 1944 and 1952 turned attention away from proteins.
Wrong cause: Bragg's order followed the failed model of November 1951, not Pauling's protein work.
Contradicted: Pauling's DNA model of 1953 shared the flaw of the first Cambridge attempt.
Outside the passage: the author never compares the two helices.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Crick concluded that the two chains of DNA run in opposite directions from
choices: the X-shaped pattern of dashes in Photo 51
the equal widths of the two kinds of base pair
Chargaff's finding that adenine always matched thymine
Donohue's correction of the forms of the bases
the crystal symmetry recorded in Franklin's report

proof.quote: the symmetry of the A form crystals, from which Crick deduced that the two chains ran in opposite directions

questions.why: Paragraph 9 says the report Perutz passed on contained the symmetry of the A form crystals, from which Crick deduced that the two chains ran in opposite directions.
distractorNotes: Wrong evidence: Photo 51 told Watson the molecule was a helix, and paragraph 12 says it did not say which way the chains ran.
Wrong step: the equal widths explained how any sequence fit between the backbones, not their direction.
Wrong step: Chargaff's ratios were explained by the pairing, not used to find the chain direction.
Wrong step: Donohue's correction led to the base pairing, not to the direction of the chains.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that a species whose DNA contained noticeably more adenine than thymine would
choices: have a correspondingly lower proportion of guanine than of cytosine
confirm the tetranucleotide hypothesis proposed by Levene
be inconsistent with the base pairing in the Watson and Crick model
have a double helix whose diameter is wider than 20 angstroms
support Pauling's three-chain structure for the molecule

proof.quote: if adenine always faces thymine, the two must be equally abundant

questions.why: Paragraph 9 says that if adenine always faces thymine, the two must be equally abundant. A species with more adenine than thymine would break that rule, so it would be at odds with the model's pairing.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: nothing links an adenine surplus to the amounts of guanine and cytosine.
Wrong paragraph: the hypothesis was about a fixed repeating order and had already fallen to Chargaff's data in paragraph 3.
Unrelated: the diameter came from Photo 51 and has nothing to do with base proportions.
Outside the passage: Pauling's model is faulted for its phosphates, not for anything about base proportions.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the Watson and Crick paper of April 1953
choices: acknowledged unpublished results from King's without saying how much had been seen
was published several months before the papers from King's College London
described two chains held together by bonds between the sugar and phosphate groups
ran to several thousand words and included Franklin's measurements in full
made no mention of any possible mechanism for copying the genetic material

proof.quote: They acknowledged being stimulated by a general knowledge of unpublished results from King's; they did not say how much they had seen.

questions.why: Paragraph 10 says they acknowledged being stimulated by a general knowledge of unpublished results from King's, and that they did not say how much they had seen.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 10 says the King's papers appeared alongside it.
Wrong detail: the chains were held together by hydrogen bonds between the paired bases, with the backbones outside.
Reversed: the paper was about nine hundred words, and the King's results were acknowledged only in general terms.
Contradicted: the paper's famous sentence proposed exactly such a copying mechanism.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that even if the Nobel committee of 1962 had wished to honor Franklin, it
choices: would have had to remove Wilkins from the list to make room for her
would have been prevented by the rules of the prize itself
would have needed the consent of Watson and Crick to do so
would have waited until her notebooks had been examined by Klug
would have awarded the prize in chemistry instead of in medicine

proof.quote: a prize is shared by at most three people and is not awarded to the dead, so the question of whether she would have been included was never put

questions.why: Paragraph 10 says a prize is shared by at most three people and is not awarded to the dead, and the previous sentence says Franklin died in 1958. Both rules stood in the way, whatever the committee thought of her work.
distractorNotes: Half right: the three-person limit is real, but she had died in 1958, so no reshuffling of the list could have included her.
Outside the passage: nothing about consent appears.
Wrong timing: Klug's reading of her notebooks is in paragraph 11 and has no connection to the committee's rules.
Outside the passage: the field of the prize is never raised as an issue.

She spent three years in Paris learning X-ray methods.
She moved to Birkbeck College and worked on viruses.
She died in 1958 at the age of thirty-seven.
She shared the 1962 Nobel Prize with Wilkins.

she had spent three years in Paris learning to apply X-ray methods
left for Birkbeck College in London, where she turned to the structure of viruses
She died of ovarian cancer in April 1958, at the age of thirty-seven.
the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to Watson, Crick, and Wilkins

questions.why: Paragraph 10 says the 1962 prize went to Watson, Crick, and Wilkins, and that Franklin, who had died in 1958, could not have been included. The other four statements come from paragraphs 5 and 10.

Paragraph 5 says she spent three years in Paris learning to apply X-ray methods.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the story in which Franklin's photograph was stolen and her discovery taken is best described as
choices: amused
unconvinced
outraged
uninterested
approving

proof.quote: That story is too simple, and I think it does her a disservice.
That is a less satisfying story than a theft or a triumph, but I suspect it is the true one.

questions.why: Paragraph 11 calls the story too simple and says it does her a disservice, and paragraph 12 prefers a less satisfying account to a theft or a triumph. The author does not accept the stolen-photograph version.
distractorNotes: Wrong register: the author treats the question of credit seriously throughout.
Too strong: the author rejects the story calmly and offers a different reading, without anger.
Reversed: the author devotes two paragraphs to the question of credit.
Reversed: the author says the story is too simple and does Franklin a disservice.

questions.stem: Which new situation best illustrates the principle described in paragraph 12?
choices: A detective solves a case from a single photograph that happens to show the culprit's face clearly
Two rival laboratories race toward the same result, and only the faster one is remembered
A surveyor refuses to publish a map until every hill has been measured twice
A search team finds a wreck where a careful sonar survey and a historian's bold guess overlap
A theorist's guess about a planet's orbit is accepted without any measurement

proof.quote: The double helix was the meeting point of two methods, the patient measurement that Franklin practiced and the bold guessing that she distrusted, and neither would have finished the job alone.
how little a single image could settle

questions.why: Paragraph 12 says the structure came from two methods meeting, patient measurement and bold guessing, and that neither would have finished the job alone. A wreck found where a careful survey and a bold guess overlap is the same pattern.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 12 opens by saying how little a single image could settle.
Wrong principle: a race between rivals is the story the author argues against, not the meeting of two methods.
Half right: patient measurement alone is one of the two methods, and the author says neither finished the job alone.
Half right: bold guessing alone is the other method, and the passage says it also could not finish the job by itself.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Watson and Crick deserve sole credit for the double helix because they alone were willing to build and test models
Rosalind Franklin solved the structure of DNA on her own, and her photograph was simply stolen by her Cambridge rivals
The structure of DNA came from several people's evidence and from two methods that needed each other
X-ray diffraction alone was enough to settle the shape of DNA once the technique had been perfected at King's
The Nobel committee of 1962 wronged Franklin by applying its rules too strictly to a case that deserved an exception

proof.quote: But the model rested on measurements made by other people
Those answers came from the symmetry in Franklin's crystallographic report, from Chargaff's ratios, from Donohue's chemistry
neither would have finished the job alone

questions.why: Paragraph 1 says the model rested on measurements made by other people, and paragraph 12 names those contributions and calls the double helix the meeting point of two methods, neither of which would have finished the job alone. One choice holds both halves.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 1 says the model rested on other people's measurements, and paragraph 12 names them.
This is the story paragraph 11 calls too simple; the passage says she was close, not finished.
Contradicted: paragraph 12 says how little a single image could settle.
Unsupported and too narrow: the Nobel rules are stated without blame, and the credit debate is only part of the passage.
